# A date, a time and a datetime written as text, run on four backends.
#
# JavaScript and Kotlin hold each as the string the literal was written as, so
# `string(d)` and `"{d}"` print it back. Go holds a time.Time, and spelled the
# conversion fmt.Sprint, which prints "2024-03-05 00:00:00 +0000 UTC" for a
# date. It now writes the literal's spelling back: 2006-01-02 for a date,
# RFC 3339 for a datetime, and HH:MM, or HH:MM:SS where it has seconds, for a
# time -- the two spellings a time literal takes.

sngl test --platform=none app.sngl
stdout 'PASS'
! stdout 'FAIL'

sngl test --platform=bubbletea --language=go app.sngl
stdout 'PASS'
! stdout 'FAIL'

sngl test --platform=html app.sngl
stdout 'PASS'
! stdout 'FAIL'

sngl test --platform=android --language=kotlin app.sngl
stdout 'PASS'
! stdout 'FAIL'

-- app.sngl --
import . "sngl:ui"
import . "sngl:test"
import time "sngl:time"

component main node {
    var d time.date = "2024-03-05"
    var t time.time = "09:30"
    var s time.time = "09:30:15"
    var dt time.datetime = "2024-03-05T09:30:00Z"
    text(value=string(d) + " {t} {s} " + string(dt))
}

func testSpelling(t Test, c main) {
    t.assert(string(c.d) == "2024-03-05")
    t.assert("{c.t}" == "09:30")
    t.assert(string(c.s) == "09:30:15")
    t.assert(string(c.dt) == "2024-03-05T09:30:00Z")
}
